title: Declarative pipelines and change-data processing
summary: Declare datasets and flows and let the graph order them; know what is incremental, rebuilt or replayed; weigh warn, drop and fail; and turn change events into type 1 and type 2 tables that survive late, tied and unplaceable changes.
outcomes: Explain datasets, flows, streaming tables, materialized views and the dependency graph, and predict what an incremental update and a full refresh read.
Choose warn, drop or fail for an expectation, and place a set-level check where it gates what the SCD tables publish.
Derive SCD type 1 and type 2 tables from change events under an explicit sequence contract, including late, tied and unplaceable changes, and test their invariants.
Map a source contract onto AUTO CDC and snapshot comparison, naming the Apache Spark release or Databricks feature that provides each capability.
startingAssumptions: The ingestion module's record resolution is known: identical redeliveries, redundant evidence, conflicts and quarantine with reasons.
The streaming module's checkpoints and micro-batches explain why a streaming read processes only new input.
SQL window functions such as ROW_NUMBER and LEAD are familiar from SQL work.
editorialRationale: Declarative pipelines are easy to demo and easy to misread, so the module first makes the graph, the incremental and rebuilt tables and the full-refresh boundary predictable, then shows what expectation actions do and cannot see, before deriving type 1 and type 2 tables from one executed event sequence with a late change, a tie and an unplaceable change. AUTO CDC and snapshot comparison come after the semantics they automate, and the module ends by placing every capability in a named Apache Spark release or in Databricks Lakeflow, because the lab's own engine has no pipelines module.

concepts.definition: The unit that reads from a source, applies a query and writes the result into one target dataset.
concepts.example: plant1 and plant2 are two append flows writing into the streaming table all_part_events.

concepts.definition: A queryable object a pipeline produces and stores or scopes: a streaming table, a materialized view or a temporary view.
concepts.example: part_events is a dataset; the flow that fills it is a separate object.

concepts.definition: The directed graph from each dataset a query reads to the dataset its flow writes, from which the pipeline derives update order.
concepts.example: cost_summary depends on part_current and supplier_history, so it updates after both.

concepts.definition: A table written by one or more streaming flows that each read only input that arrived since their checkpoint.
concepts.example: Update 2 reads eight new change rows into part_events and leaves the first five untouched.

concepts.definition: A table precomputed from exactly one batch query; in open-source Spark 4.1.0 it is truncated and rebuilt on every update.
concepts.example: supplier_names_mv reads all 18 change rows again when SUP-B is renamed and shows the new name.

concepts.definition: A refresh that clears a dataset's rows and checkpoints and recomputes it from whatever its sources still hold.
concepts.example: A 40-day-old table fed by a 30-day landing zone comes back with days 11 to 40 only.

concepts.definition: A named record-level Boolean rule on a pipeline dataset with an action for failing rows: warn and keep, drop, or fail the update.
concepts.example: known_op EXPECT (op IN ('upsert', 'delete')) with DROP ROW removes e-12, whose op is modify.

concepts.definition: A quality check that compares several rows or another table, which a single row rule cannot express.
concepts.example: GROUP BY part_id, seq HAVING more than one distinct payload finds the P-300 tie.

concepts.term: slowly changing dimension type 1 and type 2
concepts.definition: Two ways to store a changing entity: type 1 keeps only the current row per key; type 2 keeps every version with its validity interval.
concepts.example: P-100 has one type 1 row at 1310 and three type 2 rows at 1250, 1290 and 1310.

concepts.definition: The half-open range of sequence values, from a version's own sequence to the next change's, during which a type 2 row was true.
concepts.example: P-600's SUP-C row is valid from [1] to [2]; the SUP-D row from [2] onward.

concepts.definition: The source-assigned value, or ordered set of values, that says which change to one key is later, independent of arrival order.
concepts.example: Marlow orders by seq then revision_no, so (2,1) silver precedes (2,2) gold.

concepts.definition: A change that arrives after a change with a higher sequence value for the same key.
concepts.example: P-100's seq 2 arrives in batch 3, after seq 3 arrived in batch 2.

concepts.definition: Two or more different payloads for the same key at the same sequence value, which the ordering cannot place.
concepts.example: e-08 (830) and e-15 (850) both claim P-300 at seq 2.

concepts.definition: A change whose sequence value is missing or invalid, so its position among the key's changes is unknown.
concepts.example: e-09 carries seq as the string "2", so P-400's latest state cannot be known.

concepts.definition: A declarative flow that applies a change feed to a streaming table as SCD type 1 or type 2 from declared keys, sequence and delete condition.
concepts.example: KEYS (part_id) SEQUENCE BY seq APPLY AS DELETE WHEN op = 'delete' STORED AS SCD TYPE 2.

concepts.definition: Changes computed by comparing consecutive full snapshots: new or different rows become upserts and missing keys become deletes.
concepts.example: SUP-C is missing from snapshot 2, so a delete is derived at 2.

concepts.definition: The open-source declarative pipeline framework in Apache Spark from release 4.1.0, with a Python module and a spark-pipelines command.
concepts.example: from pyspark import pipelines as dp works on 4.1.0 and fails to import on 4.0.4.

concepts.definition: Databricks' managed pipeline product, which documents extensions such as expectations and AUTO CDC on top of the declarative framework.
concepts.example: Expectations with drop or fail are documented for Lakeflow and absent from the 4.1.x Python API.

concepts.definition: An external streaming destination, such as a Kafka topic, that a pipeline writes to through an append flow.
concepts.example: kafka_sink receives processed orders through the append flow kafka_orders_flow.

concepts.definition: A table property that, when false, makes the open-source engine skip a requested full refresh of that table.
concepts.example: part_events with pipelines.reset.allowed false keeps days 1 to 40 when a full refresh is requested.

concepts.definition: The change-feed row that carries a row's values before an update, committed in the same version as the postimage.
concepts.example: An update of P-100 at commit 12 yields a preimage at 1290 and a postimage at 1310.

concepts.definition: The key columns and types an AUTO CDC flow stores in its state, which later incremental runs must keep unchanged.
concepts.example: Adding plant_id to keys = ['part_id'] needs a full refresh of the target.

questions.prompt: A pipeline file contains CREATE STREAMING TABLE all_events; followed by two statements of the form CREATE FLOW plant_n AS INSERT INTO all_events SELECT * FROM STREAM(plant_n_events). How many datasets and how many flows does the file define?

options.text: One dataset and two flows: both append flows write into all_events.
options.rationale: Correct: a streaming table can receive several streaming flows, and CREATE FLOW adds a flow into an existing target rather than a new dataset.

options.text: Three datasets, because each statement creates its own table.
options.rationale: CREATE FLOW ... INSERT INTO names an existing target; it adds a flow into all_events and creates no table of its own.

options.text: One dataset and one flow, because a table can have only one writer.
options.rationale: That limit belongs to a materialized view, which has exactly one batch flow; a streaming table accepts several streaming flows.

options.text: Two datasets, one per plant, and no flow until the pipeline first runs.
options.rationale: The plant sources are read, not created, by this file, and flows exist as declarations before any run.

questions.prompt: In Cinderline's pipeline, part_current reads part_events_valid and cost_summary reads part_current and supplier_history. A developer changes part_events_valid so that it also reads cost_summary. What does spark-pipelines dry-run report?

options.text: Nothing: a dry run reads no data, so it cannot see the new dependency.
options.rationale: Reading no data is what makes a dry run cheap; the guide says it still reports analysis and graph validation errors.

options.text: An error only for part_events_valid, while the other datasets validate normally.
options.rationale: A cycle belongs to the graph, not one dataset; no update order exists for any dataset on the loop.

options.text: A graph validation error: part_events_valid, part_current and cost_summary now form a cycle.
options.rationale: Correct: the new read closes a loop through part_current, and the documented dry run catches cyclic dependencies before any data moves.

options.text: No error, and the first real run computes cost_summary from the previous update's rows.
options.rationale: The pipeline derives order from the declared queries; a loop has no valid order, so it is refused rather than resolved from old rows.

questions.prompt: part_events_named, a streaming table that joined each change with its supplier's name when it read it, holds 18 rows; supplier_names_mv, a materialized view with the same join, is rebuilt from the same 18. SUP-B is renamed and an update runs with no new files. What do you expect?

options.text: Both show the new name, because every update rereads all sources.
options.rationale: Only the materialized view is rebuilt from its query; the streaming table's checkpoint says there is nothing new to read.

options.text: The streaming table reads no rows and keeps the old name on its SUP-B rows; the view shows the new name.
options.rationale: Correct: streaming flows process each input once, while the view is recomputed from its query (truncated and rebuilt in open-source Spark 4.1.0).

options.text: Both keep the old name until the next file arrives.
options.rationale: The view does not wait for new files; each update recomputes it from the current state of its inputs.

options.text: The streaming table rewrites its 18 rows because an upstream table changed.
options.rationale: A streaming table never revisits rows it has written; rewriting them requires a full refresh.

questions.prompt: part_events_valid declares CONSTRAINT known_op EXPECT (op IN ('upsert', 'delete')) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE. Batch 2 arrives with e-12, whose op is modify, among seven valid rows. What happens?

options.text: The seven valid rows are written and e-12 is skipped.
options.rationale: Skipping the failing row while writing the rest is the drop action, not fail.

options.text: All eight rows are written and one failed expectation is counted.
options.rationale: Writing the failing row and counting it is the default warn action, not fail.

options.text: e-12's op is rewritten to upsert and the update continues.
options.rationale: An expectation never edits a row; it only keeps it, drops it or fails the update.

options.text: The update fails, so the flow writes nothing from that batch, and someone must act before it is reprocessed.
options.rationale: Correct: as Databricks documents it, fail stops the update when any row violates the rule, and the valid rows are not written by that update either.

questions.prompt: Which of these checks can be written as one expectation on part_events_valid?

options.text: unit_cost_cents is between 0 and 2147483647.
options.rationale: Correct: a Boolean condition on one row's own columns is exactly what an expectation evaluates.

options.text: No two rows share part_id and seq with different costs.
options.rationale: This needs a group of rows; each tied row passes any per-row rule on its own.

options.text: Each unit cost matches the supplier's current price list.
options.rationale: This needs another table, and a documented limit is that expectation constraints cannot query other tables.

options.text: An event_id is never delivered twice with different content.
options.rationale: This compares deliveries with one another, which is a set-level check, not a row rule.

questions.prompt: P-200's changes are seq 1 upsert (400, SUP-B) in batch 1, seq 2 delete in batch 2 and seq 3 upsert (420, SUP-C) in batch 3. What does the Type 1 table show for P-200 after batch 2 and after batch 3?

options.text: A seq 1 row at 400 after batch 2, and a seq 3 row at 420 after batch 3.
options.rationale: The delete at seq 2 is P-200's latest change after batch 2, so the key has no current row.

options.text: No row after batch 2, and still no row after batch 3, because a deleted key stays deleted.
options.rationale: A later sequence value supersedes the delete; the contract lets a part return.

options.text: No row after batch 2, and one row at seq 3 with 420 and SUP-C after batch 3.
options.rationale: Correct: the highest-sequence change decides, a delete leaves no row, and the return at seq 3 becomes current.

options.text: A row marked deleted after batch 2, and two rows after batch 3.
options.rationale: Type 1 keeps at most one row per key and holds no delete markers; history belongs in type 2.

questions.prompt: P-600 has two changes: seq 1 with supplier SUP-C and seq 2 with supplier SUP-D. Which Type 2 history satisfies the invariants?

options.text: SUP-C from 1, open; SUP-D from 2, open.
options.rationale: Two open rows for one key: the first version was never closed by the second.

options.text: SUP-C from 1 to 2; SUP-D from 2, open.
options.rationale: Correct: each version ends where the next change starts, intervals meet without overlapping, and one row is open.

options.text: SUP-C from 1 to 3; SUP-D from 2, open.
options.rationale: The intervals overlap between 2 and 3, so two versions would be true at once.

options.text: SUP-C from 2 to 1; SUP-D from 1, open.
options.rationale: An interval cannot end before it starts; this is what arrival order produces, not sequence order.

questions.prompt: e-08 and e-15 both place P-300 at seq 2, with costs 830 and 850. Which change to the pipeline resolves the tie legitimately?

options.text: Sequence by the ingestion timestamp so that the later arrival wins.
options.rationale: Ingestion time records when a copy reached you, not when the change was made, so it turns delivery accidents into history.

options.text: Break the tie by the lexical order of event_id.
options.rationale: Event ids identify deliveries; their order promises nothing about the order of business changes.

options.text: Keep the higher cost to be safe.
options.rationale: Choosing a value is a guess that hides the contract breach instead of reporting it.

options.text: Ask the source owner which field orders the two changes and, if one exists, add it as a second sequence column.
options.rationale: Correct: a STRUCT sequence breaks ties by its next field, which is legitimate only when the source assigns that field.

questions.prompt: If e-09 (P-400, seq "2", cost 95) is removed by a drop expectation before the SCD step, what does the current table publish for P-400?

options.text: The seq 1 row at 90, shown as current, with no sign that a newer change may exist.
options.rationale: Correct: the drop leaves the older valid change as the latest one, and lab L07's drop-filter test shows exactly this row.

options.text: No row, because a dropped event withholds its key.
options.rationale: A drop removes the row and leaves no mark on the key; only a quarantine policy withholds it.

options.text: The seq 2 row at 95, after the string is cast to an integer.
options.rationale: A dropped row never reaches the SCD step, and casting would guess at the contract.

options.text: A row flagged as unresolved.
options.rationale: Flags and unresolved lists come from the reference's quarantine policy; a drop keeps only a count.

questions.prompt: Which AUTO CDC declaration matches Marlow's composite contract: key customer_id, ordered by seq then revision_no, op = 'delete' marks a delete, full history kept?

options.text: KEYS (customer_id, seq) SEQUENCE BY revision_no APPLY AS DELETE WHEN op = 'delete' STORED AS SCD TYPE 2
options.rationale: Putting seq into the key makes every change a separate entity, so no customer has a history.

options.text: KEYS (customer_id) SEQUENCE BY seq APPLY AS DELETE WHEN op = 'delete' STORED AS SCD TYPE 2
options.rationale: Sequencing by seq alone leaves C-1 with two payloads at seq 2, which breaks the one-update-per-sequence-value rule.

options.text: KEYS (customer_id) SEQUENCE BY STRUCT(seq, revision_no) APPLY AS DELETE WHEN op = 'delete' STORED AS SCD TYPE 2
options.rationale: Correct: the struct orders by seq and breaks ties by revision_no, and type 2 keeps the full history.

options.text: KEYS (customer_id) SEQUENCE BY STRUCT(seq, revision_no) APPLY AS DELETE WHEN op = 'delete' STORED AS SCD TYPE 1
options.rationale: Type 1 keeps only the current row, but the requirement asks for full history.

questions.prompt: A team runs open-source Apache Spark 4.1.3 and wants a declarative pipeline with drop expectations and an SCD type 2 history built by AUTO CDC. What can you accurately tell them?

options.text: Everything they want has been in Apache Spark since 4.0.
options.rationale: The pyspark.pipelines package is absent at every 4.0.x tag; lab L07 found it not importable on 4.0.4.

options.text: 4.1.3 has declarative flows, streaming tables and materialized views, but no expectations or AUTO CDC; at 4.2.0 AUTO CDC arrives for type 1 only.
options.rationale: Correct: the 4.1.x exports contain neither, and the 4.2.0 create_auto_cdc_flow accepts only SCD type 1, so the rest means Lakeflow or their own code.

options.text: Declarative pipelines exist only on Databricks.
options.rationale: Apache Spark ships Spark Declarative Pipelines from 4.1.0, with a Python module and a command-line tool.

options.text: Upgrading to 4.2.0 gives them both expectations and SCD type 2.
options.rationale: At the 4.2.0 tag there is no expectation function and the AUTO CDC flow stores type 1 only.

selfQuestions.prompt: Cinderline fixes a parsing bug in part_events, a streaming table fed from a landing zone that keeps files for 30 days; the table has run for 40 days. An engineer proposes a full refresh. What do you ask before agreeing, and what do you propose if the answers are unfavourable?
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Ask what the refresh can re-read: it clears the table and its checkpoints, so only files still in the landing zone come back, days 11 to 40, and days 1 to 10 would disappear from the table and from everything downstream. Ask who consumes the table and whether old rows are wrong or only formatted differently. If history cannot be replayed, keep the table (pipelines.reset.allowed set to false where the engine supports it), let the fix apply to new rows, and repair old rows from a retained raw copy in a reviewed backfill.
selfQuestions.reasoning: A full refresh is only as complete as the source's retention, so protecting the table and backfilling from retained raw keeps history without guessing. Replaying from an archive is an acceptable alternative when one exists.

selfQuestions.prompt: Finance compares two history extracts of P-100, taken after batch 2 and after batch 3, and asks why a closed row changed and a new row appeared although nobody edited a price. Explain what happened and what a consumer of the history table should do.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: The seq 2 change (1290) was made before seq 3 but arrived after it. The current row did not move, because seq 3 is still the latest. History had to be corrected: the first version now ends at seq 2 instead of seq 3, and a version from seq 2 to seq 3 at 1290 was inserted. Anything computed from the older extract for that period, such as costed usage between seq 2 and seq 3, is stale and should be recomputed from the table rather than patched from the old copy.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The answer separates arrival order from sequence order and treats history as restatable, which is what an out-of-order change requires. Publishing a list of rewritten intervals for consumers is a reasonable addition.

selfQuestions.prompt: The supplier master arrives only as a weekly snapshot. A buyer says invoices showed SUP-B at 9 days of lead time for three days in March, but the history table shows 7 days throughout. Explain the discrepancy and what would change it.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: The history is derived by comparing consecutive snapshots. If SUP-B moved from 7 to 9 days and back within one week, both snapshots show 7, so no change is derived and the 9-day period never enters the history; lab L07 reproduces this by skipping snapshot 2. The table is not wrong about what the snapshots recorded, but it cannot show changes between them. Options are a more frequent snapshot, a change feed from the supplier system, or recording the invoice evidence as a separate, dated source.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The explanation locates the limit in the cadence rather than in the comparison logic, and every remedy adds observations instead of guessing values. Accepting the limit and documenting it is also defensible.

beats.title: A flow moves rows; a dataset is where they land
beats.outcome: Name the dataset and the flow that one declaration creates, and say which kind of dataset accepts more than one flow.
beats.explanation: A declarative pipeline is written as dataset definitions, not as steps. The statement that defines part_events creates two objects: a [[dbxfe-pipelines-dataset-concept|dataset]] that stores rows and a [[dbxfe-pipelines-flow-concept|flow]] that reads the landing files, applies the query and writes into it. Notice in the second state that a streaming table takes a second append flow, one per plant, while in the third a materialized view refuses any flow but its own batch query.
beats.hint: Count what a CREATE FLOW statement adds before counting tables.
beats.recap: One declaration makes a dataset that stores rows and a flow that fills it; only streaming tables take extra flows.

beats.title: The update order comes from what each query reads
beats.outcome: Derive the order and the parallel branches of a pipeline from its queries, and predict what a cycle does to validation.
beats.explanation: You never write an instruction such as run part_events before part_history. The pipeline reads each flow's query, records which datasets it reads and builds a [[dbxfe-pipelines-graph-concept|dependency graph]]: an edge from every dataset read to the dataset written. It orders and parallelizes updates along those edges. Notice in the first state that supplier_history shares no edge with the part branch until cost_summary, so both branches can run side by side. In the second, one extra read closes a loop, and a dry run refuses the graph before any data moves.

samajh.text: Socho ghar mein Diwali ki mithai ban rahi hai. Kisi ne list nahi banayi ki pehle kya karna hai; har recipe khud batati hai ki use kya chahiye. Gulab jamun ko chashni chahiye, chashni ko cheeni aur paani. Toh maa apne aap samajh jaati hai: pehle chashni, phir jamun, aur namkeen alag chulhe pe saath-saath. Par agar koi kahe ki chashni ke liye pehle gulab jamun chahiye, toh kaam wahin ruk jaata hai.
samajh.mapping: Each recipe is a dataset's query, the ingredients it names are the datasets it reads, and the order the cook works out is the dependency graph the pipeline derives.
samajh.boundary: A cook can improvise around a missing ingredient; a pipeline with a cycle or a missing table fails validation instead of guessing.

handbook.markdown:
The graph is derived, not declared. For each flow the framework analyses the query, finds the datasets it reads and draws an edge to the dataset it writes. Cinderline's graph has nine nodes and eight edges: landing files to part_events; part_events to part_events_valid and part_quarantine; part_events_valid to part_current and part_history; supplier snapshots to supplier_history; part_current and supplier_history to cost_summary. part_history and supplier_history have no path between them, so the engine may run them in parallel; cost_summary waits for both of its inputs.

A cycle has no order. If part_events_valid's query also read cost_summary, to drop parts with no supplier, cost_summary would depend on itself through part_current. The `spark-pipelines dry-run` command launches an execution that reads and writes no data but still reports three classes of error: syntax errors, analysis errors such as a missing table or column, and graph validation errors such as cyclic dependencies.

```bash
spark-pipelines dry-run --spec spark-pipeline.yml
```

The spec file, conventionally `spark-pipeline.yml`, lists the source libraries, a storage directory for checkpoints and optional catalog, database and Spark configuration entries.

The worked graph is drawn as a Lakeflow pipeline: expectations, AUTO CDC type 2 and snapshot comparison are Lakeflow features, as the editions beat shows. Under open-source spark-pipelines those three nodes become an explicit filter and tables built with window functions; the edges are the same, so the cycle and the dry run's answer do not change.

Fix a cycle by moving the shared logic upstream: a supplier-validity rule belongs in a view that part_events_valid and cost_summary both read, not in a loop back from the summary.

Limits: the graph covers datasets the pipeline defines. A table maintained by another job is a source with no incoming edge, read in whatever state it is in when the flow runs. Python that defines datasets in a loop must iterate over a list that only grows, a documented consideration, because a dataset whose definition disappears leaves the graph. What to inspect first: the dry-run output, then each flow's reads.

beats.recap: Edges come from each query's reads; independent branches run in parallel and a cycle fails validation before any data moves.

beats.title: A streaming table remembers what it read; a materialized view is rebuilt
beats.outcome: Predict how many rows a streaming table and a materialized view read on the next update, and which one reflects an upstream correction.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-pipelines-streaming-table-concept|streaming table]] is incremental: its flows keep checkpoints, so each update reads only input that arrived since and never revisits rows already written. A [[dbxfe-pipelines-mv-concept|materialized view]] answers its query again; in open-source Spark 4.1.0 it is truncated and rebuilt on every update. Notice in the second state that the streaming table reads 8 rows while the view rereads 13, and in the fourth that renaming a supplier reaches only the view.

samajh.text: Bank passbook yaad hai? Har baar branch mein sirf naye entries print hote hain; purani lines wahi rehti hain, chahe baad mein kuch bhi badle. Ab socho ek statement jo har baar poori history dobara jod ke banta hai. Passbook streaming table jaisi hai: jo padh liya, dobara nahi. Statement materialized view jaisa hai: har baar poora hisaab naye sire se, isliye koi correction ho toh wahi dikhayega.
samajh.mapping: Printing only new passbook entries is a streaming table reading from its checkpoint; recomputing the whole statement is a materialized view rebuilt from its query.
samajh.boundary: A bank corrects old entries by posting reversals; a streaming table never revisits rows it wrote unless it is fully refreshed.

handbook.markdown:
The difference is visible in the open-source engine's code. Before each update, the Apache Spark 4.1.0 `DatasetManager` truncates any existing table that is not a streaming table, so a materialized view is rebuilt by its batch query and written again. A streaming table keeps its rows, merges its schema with the new output and is written by a Structured Streaming query with its own checkpoint in append mode. Without refresh options, `spark-pipelines run` performs this default incremental update.

The consequences can be predicted with numbers. Lab L07's three batches carry 5, 8 and 5 change rows. part_events_named, a streaming table that joins each change to its supplier's name as it reads it, reads 5, then 8, then 5, and holds 18. supplier_names_mv, a materialized view with the same join, reads 5, 13 and 18. If supplier SUP-B is renamed and no file arrives, the streaming table reads 0 rows and its SUP-B rows keep the name joined when they were read; the view rereads 18 rows and shows the new name.

So choose by the question each table answers. A streaming table suits append-heavy inputs such as events and logs, where each input row is processed once and old results must not be recomputed. A materialized view suits aggregates and joins that must reflect the current state of every input, including corrections to rows already seen.

Cost follows the same line: the view's work grows with its inputs, the streaming table's with the new input. Databricks documents that its materialized views can be refreshed incrementally when its engine can do so; the result must still equal a full recompute, so reason about the view's meaning as if it were rebuilt.

Limits: a plain streaming read assumes the source only appends; a source that rewrites rows needs a change feed or options your platform documents. Changing a streaming table's query changes only rows processed afterwards.

beats.recap: A streaming table reads only new input and keeps old rows; a materialized view is recomputed, so only it reflects upstream corrections.

beats.title: A full refresh replays only what the source still holds
beats.outcome: Decide whether to full-refresh a streaming table after a logic change, given how long its sources keep data.
beats.explanation: Fixing a streaming table's query does not repair rows it already holds; only new input gets the new logic. A [[dbxfe-pipelines-full-refresh-concept|full refresh]] clears the table and its checkpoints and reads its sources from the start. That rebuilds history only if the sources still have it. Notice in the second state that a landing zone keeping 30 days of files returns days 11 to 40 on day 40: the first ten days vanish from the table and from everything downstream.
beats.hint: Compare the table's age with the source's retention before anything else.

handbook.markdown:
The command-line options make the choice explicit. `spark-pipelines run` with no options performs an incremental update. `--full-refresh part_events` clears that dataset's data and checkpoints and recomputes it from scratch; `--full-refresh-all` does so for the whole graph; `--refresh` updates named datasets without clearing anything. The 4.2.0 programming guide documents these options, and the 4.1.0 command-line code already accepts them.

```bash
spark-pipelines run --full-refresh part_events,part_history
```

Before running it, answer four questions. What does each source still hold? A landing zone with a 30-day lifecycle rule, a message topic with seven days of retention or a change feed that VACUUM has trimmed all return less than the table has seen. Who reads the table? Everything downstream is recomputed or re-fed, and a sink is worse: a full refresh resets its checkpoint but cannot recall results already written. Is the old data wrong, or merely formatted differently? A cosmetic change rarely justifies losing history. Is there a retained raw copy? A reviewed backfill from an archive is often the safer repair.

The open-source engine also lets a table refuse. With the table property `pipelines.reset.allowed` set to false, a requested full refresh of that table is skipped with a log message and a normal refresh runs instead, which protects tables whose sources cannot be replayed.

A full refresh is also the supported way to change some declarations: the 4.2.0 AUTO CDC flow keeps its key set as state and needs a full refresh of the target to change it. Limits: this beat does not cover schema changes, which the engine handles on incremental runs by merging compatible schemas into the streaming table.

beats.recap: A full refresh rebuilds only what the sources still hold, so check retention and consumers before clearing a streaming table.

beats.title: An expectation is a row rule with one of three consequences
beats.outcome: Choose warn, drop or fail for a rule and predict what each does to a bad row and to the rest of the update.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-pipelines-expectation-concept|expectation]] gives a dataset a named Boolean condition on each row and an action for rows that fail it. As Databricks documents them, warn (the default) writes the row and counts the failure, drop removes it before the write and counts it, and fail stops the update. Notice in the decision table that e-12, whose op is modify, is passed downstream, silently removed or blocks the whole batch depending on one word.
beats.hint: Ask what each action does to the other rows in the same batch.

handbook.markdown:
Expectations are declared with the dataset. In Databricks SQL (not executed here):

```sql
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE part_events_valid (
  CONSTRAINT known_op EXPECT (op IN ('upsert', 'delete')) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW,
  CONSTRAINT has_part EXPECT (part_id IS NOT NULL AND trim(part_id) <> '') ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE,
  CONSTRAINT placeable_seq EXPECT (seq IS NOT NULL AND seq > 0) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW
) AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(part_events);
```

In Python the decorators are `@dp.expect`, `@dp.expect_or_drop` and `@dp.expect_or_fail`, with `expect_all` variants taking a dictionary of rules; older examples use `import dlt` with the same names. A rule written without an ON VIOLATION clause warns, the default. State the column's type too: with seq read as INT, e-09's string "2" arrives as NULL, and `seq > 0` alone yields NULL rather than false, hence the IS NOT NULL; with seq inferred as a string, "2" > 0 is true and e-09 passes. Both behaviours were checked on local Spark 4.0.4 over the lab's rows.

Each action answers a different question. Warn keeps every row and records how many failed: right when the row is still usable and you want a trend. Drop keeps the table clean for its consumers: right when a failing row carries nothing you would act on. Fail refuses to publish: right when one bad row means the whole batch is suspect. Databricks records passing and failing counts for warn and drop in its pipeline metrics; a failed update needs attention before the data is reprocessed.

Two cautions for change data. A dropped change event is not neutral: drop e-09, whose sequence is unusable, and P-400's older price stays current with no sign that a newer change exists, as lab L07's test 10 shows. And a warned row travels on: e-12's unknown op reaches the CDC flow, where a delete condition such as op = 'delete' treats it as an update.

A common pattern keeps the evidence: invert the rules into a quarantine table that selects exactly the failing rows, so nothing is lost silently. The open-source pipelines API at the 4.1.x and 4.2.0 tags has no expectation function; this is a Databricks feature. What to inspect: failure counts per rule, and whether a drop rule's count rises without anyone reading it.

beats.recap: Warn keeps and counts, drop removes and counts, fail stops the update: one word decides where a bad row's damage goes.

beats.title: A row rule cannot see the other rows
beats.outcome: Sort quality checks into those one expectation can express and those that need a grouped or cross-table step.
beats.explanation: An expectation evaluates one row at a time and cannot query other tables. It can demand that op is upsert or delete or that seq is positive. It cannot see that e-08 and e-15 give P-300 two costs at the same sequence value, because each row is valid alone. Notice in the second state that both tied rows pass every rule; only the [[dbxfe-pipelines-set-check-concept|set-level check]] in the third state, grouping by part and sequence, finds the conflict.
beats.hint: For each check, ask how many rows it has to look at.

handbook.markdown:
Sort each check by what it must look at. One row: op in a known set, a key present, a sequence positive, a cost within range. A group of rows: one distinct payload per key and sequence value, an event id never reused with different content, no two open versions per key. Another table: a cost that matches the supplier's price list, a part that exists in the item master. Only the first kind is an expectation. The documented rule that constraints cannot query other tables excludes the third kind, and the second is invisible to any per-row test.

A grouped check is ordinary SQL, and written as a dataset it becomes part of the graph. This query was run on local Spark 4.0.4 over the lab's fifteen valid rows:

```sql
WITH payloads AS (
  SELECT part_id, seq,
         count(DISTINCT to_json(struct(op, description, unit_cost_cents, supplier_code))) AS n
  FROM part_events_valid
  GROUP BY part_id, seq
)
SELECT part_id, seq, n FROM payloads WHERE n > 1;
```

It returns one row: P-300 at seq 2 with two payloads. P-500 at seq 1 appears three times (e-05 twice and e-16) with one payload, which is redundant evidence, not a tie. Including op in the struct means an update and a delete at one sequence also count as two payloads.

Where the check sits decides what it protects. A tie view that only reads part_events_valid is a sibling of part_history: it raises an alarm and gates nothing. Lab L07's resolver gates because it recomputes both tables from every retained row, so the tie e-15 exposes in batch 3 withdraws P-300. An incremental SCD flow cannot be gated by filtering its input: e-08 applied P-300 at 830 in batch 2, and dropping e-15 in batch 3 leaves 830 current; P-400 likewise stays at 90 after e-09 is quarantined. So filter tied rows before an AUTO CDC flow to keep its input within contract, and withhold where consumers read: a withheld-keys materialized view recomputed each update and anti-joined to the published tables, or SCD tables built as materialized views over retained valid history.

The retained ingestion module owns the full classification; this beat only places it relative to expectations. What to inspect: the tie view's row count after each update, and who reads it.

beats.recap: Row rules catch malformed rows; ties, reused ids and cross-table rules need a grouped step, and withholding a key needs a table recomputed each update, not a filter on later rows.

beats.title: Type 1 keeps one row per key: the highest sequence wins
beats.outcome: Compute a Type 1 current table from ordered change events, deletes and late arrivals included.
beats.explanation: An SCD [[dbxfe-pipelines-scd-concept|type 1]] table answers one question: what is true now? For each key keep the change with the highest [[dbxfe-pipelines-sequence-concept|sequence]] value; if that change is a delete, the key has no row. Arrival order never enters. Notice in the second state that P-200 has no row after its delete, and in the third that P-100 still costs 1310 although its 1290 change arrived last: that change carries seq 2, older than seq 3.
beats.hint: Rank by sequence, not by batch.

handbook.markdown:
The rule fits one window function. Number each key's resolved changes from the highest sequence down and keep the first, unless it is a delete:

```sql
SELECT part_id, seq, description, unit_cost_cents, supplier_code
FROM (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY part_id ORDER BY seq DESC) AS rn
  FROM resolved_states
) AS ranked
WHERE rn = 1 AND op = 'upsert';
```

Filtering deletes after ranking matters: filter first and P-200 would show its seq 1 row after batch 2, a part the source had deleted. Lab L07 runs the DataFrame form of this window over three batches: five rows after batch 1, four after batch 2 (P-200 deleted, P-400 withheld) and four after batch 3 (P-200 back at seq 3, P-300 withheld by a tie). It also runs this SQL on the full event set and requires the same final rows; every result is compared with rows written by hand.

The window assumes resolved input: one row per key and sequence, no ties, every sequence valid. That is the retained ingestion module's work, done by the lab's resolver before Spark sees the rows.

An incremental engine faces one problem the batch window hides. If a delete at seq 5 arrives before an older update at seq 4, the engine must remember the delete, or the late update would bring the key back. Databricks documents how its AUTO CDC handles deletes that arrive out of order; check the current page before relying on very late data.

When to prefer type 1: operational lookups and joins that only need today's attributes. When not: any report that must show what was true earlier, which needs type 2. On Databricks the declaration is `STORED AS SCD TYPE 1`, the default. What to inspect: rows ranked first that are deletes, and keys the source still has but the table lacks.

beats.recap: Type 1 keeps the highest-sequence change per key and no row after a delete; a late, older change leaves it unchanged.

beats.title: Type 2 turns sequence values into validity intervals
beats.outcome: Build Type 2 rows with valid_from and valid_to from ordered changes, and state the invariants every history must satisfy.
beats.explanation: An SCD type 2 table keeps every accepted version with a [[dbxfe-pipelines-interval-concept|validity interval]]: valid_from is the version's sequence, valid_to the next change's sequence, and the open row is current. A delete closes the open row and opens none, leaving a gap until the key returns. Notice P-200 in the last state: 1 to 2, a gap, then 3 onward. Every history must keep at most one open row per key and no overlapping intervals.
beats.hint: valid_to comes from the next change, whatever kind it is.

handbook.markdown:
LEAD computes the interval, and it must see the delete rows before they are filtered out:

```sql
SELECT part_id, valid_from, valid_to, valid_to IS NULL AS is_current,
       description, unit_cost_cents, supplier_code
FROM (
  SELECT *, seq AS valid_from,
         LEAD(seq) OVER (PARTITION BY part_id ORDER BY seq) AS valid_to
  FROM resolved_states
) AS ordered
WHERE op = 'upsert';
```

Intervals are half-open: a row is true for sequence values s with valid_from ≤ s < valid_to. Written that way, versions meet without overlapping, and an as-of lookup has exactly one answer:

```sql
WHERE part_id = 'P-100' AND valid_from <= 2 AND (valid_to IS NULL OR 2 < valid_to)
```

After batch 3 that returns P-100's 1290 version.

Two invariants make a history trustworthy, and lab L07 checks both on every table it produces: at most one open row per key, and per key no interval that ends before it starts or overlaps the next. The checks catch structural damage, such as a second open row or a stretched interval, and the lab proves that by breaking three tables on purpose. They cannot catch a wrong but well-formed value; the hand-written literals do that.

AUTO CDC on Databricks writes the same interval as `__START_AT` and `__END_AT`, typed like the sequencing column, and documents an option to track history on only some columns, so that a change in an untracked column updates the current version instead of opening a new one.

A sequence is not a date. To answer what a part cost on 3 March, the history must be sequenced by a timestamp the source assigns, or joined to one. When not to use type 2: attributes nobody queries historically, where the extra rows only add storage and join care.

beats.recap: Type 2 keeps every version with a half-open interval; at most one open row and no overlaps per key.

beats.title: A late change rewrites history but not the present
beats.outcome: Predict the edits a late-arriving change forces on the current and history tables.
beats.explanation: P-100's seq 2 change is a [[dbxfe-pipelines-late-concept|late-arriving change]]: it arrives in batch 3, after seq 3. The current row does not move, because seq 3 is still the highest. History must change twice: the version that ran from 1 to 3 now ends at 2, and a new row runs from 2 to 3. Notice in the third state what an append-only history does instead: it writes a row from 3 to 2, which the interval check rejects.
beats.hint: Place the change by its sequence first, then ask which interval it splits.

handbook.markdown:
Between batch 2 and batch 3 lab L07 compares whole rows. Current loses P-300, which a tie withdraws, and gains P-200 at seq 3; P-100's current row is unchanged. History loses P-100 1 to 3 and both P-300 rows, and gains P-100 1 to 2, P-100 2 to 3 and P-200 from 3. One late change forced an update of a closed row and an insert between two existing rows.

That has three consequences for a production pipeline. First, the history table cannot be append-only; whatever maintains it must update rows it has already published. AUTO CDC documents that it handles out-of-order records by their sequence, which is this work done incrementally. Second, anyone who copied the history before the late change holds a stale extract: a report that costed P-100's usage between seq 2 and seq 3 at 1250 is now wrong, and nothing in the copy says so. Third, the problem is measurable: count late changes per update and how far behind the latest sequence each one lands.

The naive design fails loudly here, which is useful. The starter's append-per-arrival function closes the open row at each arrival: P-100 opens at 1, closes at 3 when seq 3 arrives, opens at 3, then closes at 2 when seq 2 arrives. The lab's test asserts the exact failure:

```python
with self.assertRaises(ScdContractError) as raised:
    check_intervals(append_per_arrival(EVENTS), "part_id")
self.assertEqual(raised.exception.reason, "interval_order")   # P-100, row from [3] to [2]
```

How to explain it to a stakeholder: nobody edited a price; a change made before the current one arrived after it, and the history now shows when each price was actually in force. What to inspect: rows whose valid_to changed between two extracts, which is the list of restated periods.

beats.recap: A late, older change leaves the current row alone but shortens a closed version and inserts one, so history must be updatable.

beats.title: Two payloads at one sequence value are a contract breach, not a coin toss
beats.outcome: Detect a tie on the sequence key and choose between withholding the key and adding a tie-breaker the source actually assigns.
beats.explanation: A sequence can order changes only if each key has at most one distinct payload per value. e-08 says P-300 costs 830 at seq 2; e-15 says 850 at seq 2. That is a [[dbxfe-pipelines-tie-concept|tied sequence value]]: nothing in the rows says which is later, so the lab withholds P-300 rather than let arrival order decide. Notice in the second state that Marlow's tie disappears once the contract orders by seq and then revision_no, a field its source assigns.

samajh.text: Ek chemist ke paas ek hi mareez ki do parchiyan aayi, dono pe same date, par dose alag: ek pe 5 mg, doosri pe 10 mg. Kaunsi nayi hai? Parchi pe kuch nahi likha. Samajhdar chemist andaaza nahi lagata; dawai rok ke doctor ko phone karta hai. Agar doctor parchi pe time bhi likhta, toh sawaal hi nahi uthta. Jo pehle counter pe pahunchi, uska koi matlab nahi.
samajh.mapping: The two prescriptions are two payloads at one sequence value, the doctor's written time is a tie-breaker the source assigns, and the order they reached the counter is arrival order.
samajh.boundary: A chemist can phone the doctor at once; a pipeline withholds the key and lists it until the source owner issues a correction, which may take days.

handbook.markdown:
Databricks' AUTO CDC documentation asks for one distinct update per key at each sequencing value and accepts a STRUCT as the sequence, ordered by its first field and then by the next when the first ties. That is the legitimate fix when the source has a second ordering field:

```sql
SEQUENCE BY STRUCT(seq, revision_no)
```

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import struct

sequence_by = struct("seq", "revision_no")
```

Marlow numbers corrections within one change: m-03 (silver) is revision 1 of change 2 and m-04 (gold) revision 2. Ordered by both, C-1 has three versions ending in gold, and m-08, which repeats m-04 under a new event id, is redundant evidence. Ordered by seq alone, the same rows tie and lab L07 withholds C-1, publishing only C-2.

Illegitimate tie-breakers are tempting because they always produce an answer. Ingestion time records when a copy reached you, so it turns delivery accidents into business history. Event id order is lexical, not temporal. Keeping the higher cost is a guess dressed as a policy. Each hides the breach instead of reporting it.

Not every repeat is a tie. Two deliveries with the same payload at the same key and sequence are redundant evidence and count once; P-500's e-05 and e-16 are the example. Only different payloads tie, which is why the lab compares payloads without delivery fields such as event id and batch.

Tie handling is policy, so write it down: withhold the key and list it (the lab's choice), block the whole publication (the retained module's gate), or route the pair to an owner who issues a new, higher sequence. Settle ties before rows reach an AUTO CDC flow; this course makes no claim about how that engine treats one. What to inspect: the grouped tie check's output after each update.

beats.recap: A tie is two payloads at one sequence value; withhold the key or add a tie-breaker the source assigns, never arrival order.

beats.title: Dropping an unplaceable change is a decision about the current row
beats.outcome: Explain why a change with an invalid sequence value withholds its key instead of being dropped, and what dropping would publish.
beats.explanation: e-09 says P-400 now costs 95, but its sequence is the string "2", not an integer. It is an [[dbxfe-pipelines-unplaceable-concept|unplaceable change]]: it might be P-400's latest state, and nothing can tell. Notice in the second state what each policy publishes. The lab's reference withholds P-400 and names the reason. Dropping the row first publishes P-400 at its seq 1 price, 90, as if current, and P-700, whose only change was unreadable, vanishes without a trace.
beats.hint: Ask whether the dropped row could have been the latest state of a key.

handbook.markdown:
The principle is the retained ingestion module's: a known key with an unreadable change cannot prove its current version, so it is not published as if it could. What this module adds is where the damage shows in SCD tables. In type 1, a dropped change leaves an older row current. In type 2, it leaves the older version open, and every as-of query after the lost change returns it.

Lab L07 measures both policies on the same fifteen valid rows. The reference quarantines e-09, e-12 and e-17 with their reasons (invalid_sequence, invalid_op, missing_part_id), withholds P-400, excludes P-700 and lists both. The drop filter publishes five current rows including P-400 at 90, reports no quarantine and no exclusion, and still withholds P-300, because a tie is not a row-level failure.

```python
kept = [e for e in EVENTS if not reasons(e, CINDERLINE)]   # what a drop rule leaves behind
```

Declarative engines hand the same decision to you. AUTO CDC documents that NULL sequencing values are unsupported, so a row whose sequence cannot be parsed must be routed out before the flow. Routing it into a quarantine table keeps the evidence; a drop expectation keeps only a count. Routing it out keeps the flow's input valid but withholds nothing on its own: P-400's seq 1 row was applied before e-09 arrived, so an incremental target still shows 90 until a table recomputed each update, such as a withheld-keys view that consumers join, takes P-400 out.

A withheld key needs a visible status. Publish the number of withheld keys beside the table and give each an owner: the source team corrects the sequence, and the corrected change arrives through the ordinary path with a valid, higher sequence.

Dropping is acceptable when the row can carry no state for a known key: a heartbeat, a test message, a row whose key is blank. e-17 is such a row; it is quarantined, but it withholds nothing. What to inspect: quarantined rows that name keys with published state, which are the keys whose current row may be stale.

beats.recap: An unplaceable change withholds its key; dropping it silently publishes the older state as current.

beats.title: AUTO CDC declares keys, sequence and deletes; the engine keeps the order
beats.outcome: Translate a source contract into an AUTO CDC declaration and name the duties it leaves upstream.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-pipelines-autocdc-concept|AUTO CDC]] flow, formerly APPLY CHANGES, turns the lab's reference into a declaration: the keys, the sequence expression, the condition that marks a delete, the columns to keep and the SCD type. The engine then applies each batch incrementally, out-of-order changes included. Notice in the second state that three duties of the reference have no clause: quarantine with reasons, the tie policy and unplaceable changes. They stay upstream, in your pipeline and your contract.
beats.hint: Match each clause to one promise in the source contract.

handbook.markdown:
On Databricks the declaration is a streaming table plus a flow. SQL, not executed here, with names as the author recalled them from the AUTO CDC documentation:

```sql
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE part_history;

CREATE FLOW part_history_cdc AS AUTO CDC INTO part_history
FROM STREAM(part_events_valid)
KEYS (part_id)
APPLY AS DELETE WHEN op = 'delete'
SEQUENCE BY seq
COLUMNS * EXCEPT (op, seq, event_id, batch)
STORED AS SCD TYPE 2;
```

Python, for Marlow's composite contract:

```python
from pyspark import pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql.functions import expr, struct

dp.create_streaming_table("customer_history")
dp.create_auto_cdc_flow(
    target="customer_history",
    source="customer_events_valid",
    keys=["customer_id"],
    sequence_by=struct("seq", "revision_no"),
    apply_as_deletes=expr("op = 'delete'"),
    except_column_list=["op", "seq", "revision_no", "event_id", "batch"],
    stored_as_scd_type=2,
)
```

Map it onto lab L07: the contract's key is KEYS, its sequence columns are SEQUENCE BY, the op field drives APPLY AS DELETE, and valid_from and valid_to become `__START_AT` and `__END_AT`. The engine applies changes incrementally where the lab recomputes everything, and sequences late changes into history for you.

What it does not do is just as concrete. It does not quarantine with reasons; validate upstream and keep the failures. It expects one distinct update per key per sequence value and does not support NULL sequencing, so ties and unplaceable changes must be settled first. Settling them upstream keeps its input within contract, but a filter on later rows cannot take back a key the target already applied; withhold such keys where consumers read, as the row-rules beat shows. And its state is durable: the open-source 4.2.0 docstring says the key set is persisted, and changing it needs a full refresh of the target.

Open-source Spark differs by release. At the 4.2.0 tag `create_auto_cdc_flow` exists in Python, needs a target made with `create_streaming_table` and accepts only SCD type 1, and the SQL grammar has no AUTO CDC statement. So the type 1 half of this lab maps onto open-source 4.2.0 and none of it onto 4.1.x. To demonstrate honestly, show the lab's executed tables first, then the declaration labelled as an unexecuted adaptation.

beats.recap: AUTO CDC declares keys, sequence, deletes and SCD type; validation, ties and unplaceable changes remain your upstream duties.

beats.title: A snapshot comparison sees states, never the changes between them
beats.outcome: Derive changes from consecutive snapshots and say what the snapshot cadence hides.
beats.explanation: Some sources send no change events, only full [[dbxfe-pipelines-snapshot-concept|snapshots]]. Comparing each snapshot with the one before yields upserts for rows that are new or different, deletes for keys that vanished and nothing for unchanged rows. Notice in the last state that without snapshot 2, SUP-B's 9-day lead time never appears: it changed and changed back between the two snapshots kept, and SUP-C's delete moves to snapshot 3. Only a finer cadence would show more.

samajh.text: Society ke notice board ki har Sunday photo li jaati hai. Budhwar ko kisi ne notice lagaya aur Shukravar ko hata diya, toh woh kisi photo mein nahi aayega; record ke hisaab se woh kabhi laga hi nahi. Aur jo notice Sunday ki photo se gayab hai, use hata hua tabhi maano jab poora board photo mein aaya ho, aadha nahi.
samajh.mapping: Each Sunday photo is a snapshot, a notice put up and taken down between photos is a change no comparison can see, and a half-framed photo is an incomplete snapshot.
samajh.boundary: A photo can be retaken the same day; a missed snapshot of a source system usually cannot be recovered later.

handbook.markdown:
Lab L07's `snapshot_changes` implements the comparison in plain Python: for each snapshot in order, every key in the previous or the current snapshot is checked; a row that appears or differs becomes an upsert sequenced by the snapshot number, and a missing key becomes a delete. Three supplier snapshots yield eight changes, four at 1, three at 2 and one at 3, and the resulting history gives SUP-B three versions (7, 9 and 7 days) and closes SUP-C at 2.

Databricks automates the comparison as AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT, a Python API that takes a snapshot source and keys and stores SCD type 1 or type 2 (not executed here; names as the author recalled them). Its source can be a table holding the latest snapshot, compared at each update, or a function that returns successive snapshots with their versions, which is how older snapshots are replayed in order.

Three limits apply to any snapshot comparison, automated or not. It sees only what a snapshot recorded: SUP-B's 9-day period exists only if snapshot 2 was taken. It dates each change to the first snapshot that shows it, not to when it happened, so intervals are only as precise as the cadence. And absence means deletion only if the snapshot is complete: a partial export that omits a supplier through a filter bug would close that supplier's history. Confirm completeness with the source owner before treating absence as a delete.

Snapshots also cost more to process than change events, because every comparison reads the whole snapshot. Prefer a change feed when the source can provide one, and use snapshots when it cannot.

What to inspect: the change count per snapshot, sudden bursts of deletes, and the gap between snapshot dates whenever someone asks about a change that fell between them.

beats.recap: Snapshot comparison yields upserts and deletes per snapshot, but a change that reverts between snapshots is never seen.

beats.title: Name the release before you name the feature
beats.outcome: Place a pipeline capability in Apache Spark 4.0.4, 4.1.x, 4.2.0 or Databricks Lakeflow before promising it.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-pipelines-sdp-concept|Apache Spark Declarative Pipelines]] ships in open-source Spark from 4.1.0: flows, streaming tables, materialized views, sinks and the spark-pipelines command. It is absent from 4.0.4, the lab's engine. At the 4.2.0 tag the Python API adds an AUTO CDC flow that stores SCD type 1 only. Expectations, type 2 through AUTO CDC and snapshot CDC are documented for [[dbxfe-pipelines-lakeflow-concept|Lakeflow]] pipelines on Databricks. Notice in the matrix that every cell cites a release or a document.
beats.hint: Separate what a release's own source exports from what a platform documents.

handbook.markdown:
The evidence method matters as much as the answer. For open source, read the release itself: the `pyspark.pipelines` package and its programming guide are absent at every 4.0.x tag and present at v4.1.0; the package exports `append_flow`, `create_streaming_table`, `materialized_view`, `table`, `temporary_view` and `create_sink` at v4.1.0 and v4.1.3; at v4.2.0 it adds `create_auto_cdc_flow`, whose docstring accepts only SCD type 1; and neither the 4.1.0 nor the 4.2.0 SQL grammar parses an AUTO CDC statement or an EXPECT constraint. The Spark project lists 4.1.0 through 4.2.0 among its stable releases.

Lab L07 checked its own engine rather than trusting a version string:

```python
importlib.util.find_spec("pyspark.pipelines") is None   # True on PySpark 4.0.4
```

For Databricks, read its documentation: expectations with warn, drop and fail; AUTO CDC for type 1 and type 2 in SQL and Python; AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT in Python; incremental materialized view refresh where the engine can do it. Databricks describes its Lakeflow pipelines as extending Spark Declarative Pipelines; its current Python examples import the same `pyspark.pipelines` module as `dp`, while older ones use `import dlt`, from the product's former name, Delta Live Tables.

Three practical rules follow. Ask for the exact Spark release before discussing features: 4.1.3 and 4.2.0 differ on AUTO CDC. Say which parts of a design are open-source semantics (the graph, streaming tables, materialized views) and which are platform features. And keep the core logic portable where you can: the SCD tables in lab L07 are plain window functions that run on any Spark 4.x.

Limits: this matrix records the releases checked on 2026-09-23. Later releases may add capabilities, and Databricks' documentation changes independently of Apache releases.

beats.recap: Check the exact release: pipelines arrive in Spark 4.1.0, AUTO CDC type 1 at 4.2.0, and expectations and type 2 are Lakeflow features.

extensionCards.prompt: How does a declarative pipeline write to a Kafka topic instead of a table, and what can a full refresh undo there?
extensionCards.answer: It declares a sink with create_sink and feeds it through an append flow; a full refresh resets the sink's checkpoint but cannot remove results already written.
extensionCards.explanation: A [[dbxfe-pipelines-extension-sinks-concept|pipeline sink]] is an external streaming destination such as a Kafka topic or an Azure Event Hubs topic. The 4.2.0 programming guide documents three limits: sinks accept only streaming writes through append flows, are defined only in the Python API, and are append-only. A full refresh resets the sink's checkpoint but does not clean previously written results, so a replayed flow writes the same messages again. Downstream consumers therefore need their own idempotency, keyed by something stable such as the event id. create_sink is already exported at the 4.1.0 tag.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: A full refresh is reversible for tables but not for messages already delivered, so sink consumers must tolerate replays.

extensionCards.prompt: How can a table be protected from an accidental full refresh in open-source Spark Declarative Pipelines?
extensionCards.answer: Set its table property pipelines.reset.allowed to false; a requested full refresh then skips that table, logs why and refreshes it normally.
extensionCards.explanation: The Apache Spark 4.1.0 engine recognizes [[dbxfe-pipelines-extension-reset-concept|pipelines.reset.allowed]], default true. When a run asks for a full refresh of a table whose property is false, the engine moves that table from the full-refresh set to the ordinary refresh set and logs that the full refresh was skipped. The table keeps its rows and checkpoints; new input still flows in. That protects tables whose sources cannot be replayed, such as a landing zone with short retention, and makes repairing them a deliberate backfill instead of a side effect of a command-line flag.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: One property turns an irreversible loss of history into a skipped step with a log line.

extensionCards.prompt: Which Delta change data feed rows must be removed before the feed drives an SCD flow, and why?
extensionCards.answer: The update_preimage rows: each carries the old values in the same commit version as its postimage, so keeping both creates a tie at one sequence value.
extensionCards.explanation: A Delta change data feed labels every change row with _change_type (insert, update_preimage, update_postimage or delete) and the _commit_version of its commit. An update produces two rows, the [[dbxfe-pipelines-extension-preimage-concept|update_preimage]] with the values before and the postimage with the values after, both at the same commit version. Sequenced by _commit_version, the pair is two payloads for one key at one sequence value: exactly the tie the sequence contract forbids. Filter preimages out, treat delete rows as deletes, and remember that change records expire with the table's retention.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Feeding one table's change feed into another's SCD flow is common, and the preimage rows silently create ties.

extensionCards.prompt: Why can't the keys of an open-source Spark AUTO CDC flow be changed between incremental runs?
extensionCards.answer: The key set and its types are part of the flow's persisted state; the 4.2.0 docstring calls a change undefined behaviour and requires a full refresh of the target.
extensionCards.explanation: An AUTO CDC flow matches each incoming change to a target row by its keys and keeps state between runs to do so incrementally. The Apache Spark 4.2.0 docstring of create_auto_cdc_flow states that the set and types of [[dbxfe-pipelines-extension-keys-concept|persisted AUTO CDC keys]] are part of that state: renaming, swapping, adding, removing or retyping a key column across incremental runs is unsupported and undefined. Changing the key set requires a full refresh of the target, which in turn is limited by what the source still holds. Choose keys from the source contract before the first run.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: A key chosen casually on day one can only be changed later by a full refresh that may lose history.

recap.title: Declare the tables, then defend the sequence
recap.markdown: **A declarative pipeline is a graph of datasets and flows, and a change table is only as good as its sequence contract.** Streaming tables read each input once; materialized views are rebuilt; a full refresh returns only what the sources still hold. Expectations judge one row at a time: warn passes the damage on, drop hides it, fail stops the update, and none of them sees a tie. Type 1 keeps the highest-sequence change per key; type 2 turns sequences into half-open intervals that a late change restates. A tie or an unplaceable change withholds its key instead of letting arrival order decide. AUTO CDC declares keys, sequence and deletes, but validation and tie policy stay with you, and every feature needs a named release. **Transfer challenge:** a clinic's booking system sends appointment changes with a per-booking version, duplicate versions after a failover and nightly full exports of clinician rosters. Design the type 1 and type 2 tables, the expectations with their actions and the tie policy, then say which parts would run on open-source Spark 4.2.0.

appliedTask.title: Build the gauge calibration history and keep the evidence honest
appliedTask.prompt: Cinderline's calibration system sends change events per gauge: gauge_id, cal_seq, a correction_no assigned only since March, op (upsert or delete) and the measured tolerance. Last week's feed holds a late cal_seq 7 for gauge G-12 that arrived after cal_seq 9, two different payloads for G-30 at cal_seq 4 from February, and one event whose cal_seq is empty. The certificate list arrives as a monthly full snapshot. Quality wants the current tolerance per gauge and the tolerance in force at any past calibration. Describe the datasets and flows, the rules with their actions, the sequence contract, the SCD tables and what they show for G-12 and G-30, what the monthly snapshot hides, and which parts would run on open-source Spark 4.1.3.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: Graph: landing files feed gauge_events (streaming table), then gauge_events_valid with expectations and a quarantine table of failing rows; a tie check groups by gauge_id and cal_seq; gauge_current (type 1) and gauge_history (type 2) read a view that drops rows at tied values, which keeps an AUTO CDC input within contract. That filter cannot take back a gauge the incremental tables already applied, so a withheld-gauges materialized view, recomputed each update from the tie check and the quarantine, is anti-joined into the tables Quality reads (or, as in lab L07, both SCD tables are materialized views recomputed from retained valid history); certificate_history comes from comparing monthly snapshots. Rules: a blank gauge_id goes to quarantine: it names no gauge, so it withholds nothing, and failing the update would stop every good row with it; an unknown op and an empty or non-positive cal_seq are routed to quarantine rather than dropped, and the empty-cal_seq event withholds the gauge it names. Contract: sequence by (cal_seq, correction_no) from March; February ties have no tie-breaker, so G-30 is withheld and listed. G-12: current stays at cal_seq 9; in history, the version that ran from G-12's previous calibration up to 9 now ends at 7, and a version from 7 to 9 is inserted. The monthly snapshot hides certificates issued and revoked within a month and dates each change to the snapshot that first shows it. On 4.1.3 the graph, streaming tables, materialized views and tie check run; expectations and AUTO CDC do not, so validation is an explicit filter and the SCD tables are window functions, with AUTO CDC declarations kept as unexecuted Databricks adaptations.
appliedTask.reasoning: The answer validates upstream and withholds keys where consumers read, because an incremental SCD target cannot take back a gauge it already applied; it predicts the late change's restatement exactly, withholds the key whose tie has no source-assigned breaker, names the cadence limit, and separates open-source 4.1.3 capabilities from Databricks features.
